latin.2061: THESIS I. COmmunis & recepta Theologorum doctrina est, eaque ex Scripturae manifestis documentis hausta, aeternam Dei voluntatem esse rerum omnium causam; ac immutabilibus providentiae Divinae Decretis omnia subjacere, etiam actus humanos; neque quicquam, non tantum a causis brutis sive inanimis, sed etiam ab hominibus & Angelis fieri, nisi secundum aeternam Dei praeordinationem & determinationem.
latin.2062: II. Inde autem omnino perire videtur libertas, tam in Angelis quam in hominibus. Nec enim ullus divinae voluntati resistere potest. Adeoque si Deus vult Angelos & homines id agere quod agunt, aliter agere non possunt, & sic libere non agunt, nec sunt actuum suorum Domini. Deinde si voluntatis humanae actiones immutabilibus Dei decretis determinatae sunt, tolli videtur omnis voluntatis indeterminatio, & in agendo indifferentia, in qua ratio libertatis consistit.
latin.2063: III. Haec difficultas tam ardua visa est Scholasticis nonnullis, ut hac in parte suam ignorantiam ingenue fassi sunt, & existimaverint rem esse quae superat mentis humanae captum, quamdiu mortali hoc corpore gravatur. Quo de numero fuit Cardinalis Cajetanus inter Scholasticos vir admodum celebris. Is enim, quantumvis acutus & subtilis, hac in re nunquam sibi potuit satisfacere, & putavit concordiam liberi arbitrii cum divina providentia, in hac vita esse inexplicabilem & non intelligibilem, ut videre est in ejus commentariis in primam partem Thomae, quaest. 22. art. 4.
latin.2064: IV. Alii tamen Scholae Romanae Theologi confidunt hunc nodum se solvere posse, & in hunc finem varia conquirunt & comminiscuntur. Nec enim idem omnes censent, vel de Decretis Divinis, vel de ratione libertatis humanae.
latin.2065: V. Et primo quidem qui dicuntur Thomistae recentiores docent quaecunque in mundo contingunt & geruntur, ac proinde etiam liberos voluntatis actus, sigillatim a Deo praedeterminata & praedefinita esse, idque absoluta & efficaci voluntate, prius ratione quam Deus ullam voluntatis creatae determinationem praevideret, sive absolute, sive sub conditione futuram. Haec est expressa sententia inter alios Didaci Alvarez Archiepiscopi Tranensis & Salpensis in summa Operis de auxiliis divinae gratiae, libro secundo, capite quinto, quod incipit his verbis, Ex divinis literis, si attente perpendantur, habemus quod Deus sua absoluta & efficaci voluntate praedeterminavit omnes actus etiam liberos in particulari, futuros in tempore, prius in signo rationis, quam intellectus divinus cognosceret actus illos esse futuros, etiam ex hypothesi quod voluntas creata constitueretur in tali ordine rerum, & in talibus circumstantiis.
latin.2066: VI. Eandem doctrinam tradit Matthaeus de Rispolis in tractatu cui titulus est, Status controversiae praedefinitionum & praedeterminationum cum libero arbitrio. Ibi enim libro primo quaestione prima, multis docet & probare contendit in Deo dari praedefinitiones & praedeterminationes aeternas actuum voluntatis, idque in particulari, & decreto absoluto, quod nullam praesupponit scientiam conditionatam futurae determinationis ipsius voluntatis, si collocetur in tali rerum statu. Et his quoque consentit Gulielmus Estius ut manifeste colligitur ex iis quae apud ipsum leguntur ad distinctionem trigesimam nonam libri primi sententiarum, & ad vigesimam quartam libri secundi.
latin.2067: VII. Nec ab hac aeterna Dei praedeterminatione excipiunt authores illi malos ipsos voluntatis actus, quos etiam absoluto & efficaci decreto praedefinitos esse volunt, saltem quantum ad illud quod in istis actibus est reale atque positivum; malitiam enim ipsam, quae non aliud est quam debitae rectitudinis privatio, non efficaciter a Deo decretam, sed solum permissam esse confitentur. Istud praesertim videre est apud Didacum Alvares in citata jam summa de auxiliis libro secundo capite nono, cujus hoc est initium, Quae dicta sunt de praedeterminatione voluntatis ad actus bonos, extendi debent ad actum peccati in quantum actus & ens est. Unde quicquid entitatis reperitur in quocunque actu peccati, etiamsi alias sit intrinsece malus, debet reduci in Deum tanquam in primam causam praemoventem & praedeterminantem voluntatem creatam ad talem actum, in quantum actus est, & secundum quod est ens.
latin.2068: VIII. Quanquam autem Deus, ex eorum mente, aeterno suo decreto praedeterminaverit & praedefinierit quaecunque in tempore a causis quibuslibet fiunt, istud nihil obstare pertendunt quominus multa non necessario, sed contingenter & libere fiant: quoniam aeterna Dei providentia non omnibus eventibus & effectibus praeparavit causas necessarias, sed quibusdam causas liberas, sive contingentes; neque solum determinavit hoc vel illud fieri, sed etiam modum quo res quaeque fieret, adeoque voluit ut quaedam necessario, alia vero contingenter & libere fierent. Et sic tantum abest ut aeterna Dei Providentia libertatem tollat actuum humanorum, ut contra quicquid est in rebus libertatis & contingentiae ad ipsum tanquam ad causam primam referendum sit: quia, scilicet, Deus non tantum res esse voluit, sed etiam voluntate sua statuit & definivit modum & rationem quo singulae esse deberent.
latin.2069: IX. Itaque quod Deus ab aeterno decrevit ut homines hoc aut illud agerent, & voluntate sua in haec vel illa objecta ferrentur, juxta sensum istorum Doctorum nihil hominum libertati officit: quia Deus non simpliciter decrevit ut hoc aut illud agerent, sed etiam ut libere agerent, id est, ut ex propriae rationis judicio hoc vel illud tanquam sibi maxime conveniens & commodum eligerent, & quidem ita ut ex diverso judicio oppositum eligere possent, qua in re, juxta eorum sententiam, proprie consistit libertas humana, quam proinde non evertit decreti divini determinatio.
latin.2070: X. Censent enim, ut loquuntur, impertinens esse libero arbitrio utrum suam electionem sibi impressam habeat a causa priori, an non: modo electio illa fiat ex judicio intellectus practici, qui diversas boni rationes circa opposita possit considerare, & voluntati proponere.
latin.2071: XI. Quod si quis dicat nomen liberi arbitrii designare causam independentem ab aliqua priori, respectu liberae suae actionis, respondent istud falso & immerito tanquam verum assumi, & ejusmodi liberum arbitrium soli Deo competere, qui omnino est a causa superiori independens. Creaturas vero liberas non minus in suis actibus liberis a prima Causa pendere, quam causas necessarias in actibus necessariis.
latin.2072: XII. Ad id vero quod objicitur, posito decreto divino circa aliquem actum humanae voluntatis, voluntatem humanam non posse aliter agere, adeoque tolli ejus in agendo indifferentiam, in qua posita est libertas, respondent, non quidem simul consistere ut Deus decreverit voluntatem aliquid agere, istud vero voluntas non agat, aut aliter agat: sed tamen decretum Dei non obstare quominus in voluntate maneat potestas aliter agendi: quoniam decretum Dei actum quidem determinat, sed facultatem relinquit flexibilem ad oppositum. Ac proinde quum homo juxta Dei decretum aliquid agit, vere dici potest illum posse non agere, & aliter agere, quia, videlicet, Deus decrevit quidem ut hoc agat, sed tamen ita agat ut potens maneat aliter agendi: Adeoque, licet in sensu composito verum non sit, posito decreto Divino voluntatem posse agere, vel non agere, verum est tamen in sensu diviso: quia cum decreto Divino non consistit quidem actus oppositus, sed optime tamen consistit facultas ad actum oppositum.
latin.2073: XIII. Quod si aliquis urgeat, posito decreto Divino de actione aliqua, nullo modo posse dici hominem posse aliter agere, quoniam inde sequeretur decreta Dei posse frustrari & irrita esse, quod simpliciter impossibile est, negant istam consequentiam, quia si homo aliter ageret, quod supponitur possibile, Deus aliter decrevisset. Nec pugnare existimant cum immutabilitate decretorum divinorum quod homo dum illa exequitur, potestatem servat aliter agendi, sed solum si quis dicat, contingere posse ut homo contrarium agat ejus quod a Deo decretum est, id quod Theologi isti minime dicunt.
latin.2074: XIV. His similia multa legere est apud Gulielmum Estium locis ante citatis & apud Didacum Alvarez in summa de Auxiliis libro secundo capite sexto, ubi dissolvit objectiones contra praedeterminationem voluntatis ex decreto Dei extrinseco provenientem. Ad illud enim quod sibi objicit ex ejus sententia sequi hominem non posse velle, nisi id quod Deus efficaci decreto vult eum velle: nec posse operari nisi actus praedeterminatos a Deo; adeoque nos non libere velle id quod volumus, sed ex necessitate absoluta, quia non possumus aliter facere, si Deus vult ut faciamus illud, Et eadem ratione non libere omitti a nobis eos actus qui sunt in praecepto: Quia si necessarium est ad hoc ut talem actum faciamus, ut Deus praedeterminaverit voluntatem nostram ad eundem actum, illum facere non possumus, si Deus suo decreto absoluto & efficaci non praedeterminavit actum illum fieri a nobis. Respondet, quod sicut aliud est posse currere, aliud vero actu currere; ita aliud est posse velle, vel producere actum aliquem in particulari; aliud autem de facto illum producere: ut ergo homo vere possit velle aliquod objectum, non requiri quod ex aeternitate praecesserit in Deo absolutum & efficax decretum praedeterminans ejus liberum arbitrium ad volendum idem objectum; quamvis id requiratur ut illud actu velit. Unde ex hoc quod in Deo non fuerit hujusmodi decretum, non sequi quod homo non possit velle tale objectum absolute loquendo: sed solum sequi quod de facto non velit illud. Nec etiam sequi quod, si Deus praedeterminavit me ad volendum hoc in particulari, non sit, absolute loquendo, in mea potestate aliud velle; quamvis ex suppositione divinae voluntatis efficacis, impossibile sit in sensu composito quod velim aliud objectum.
latin.2075: XV. Ad id vero quod objicitur praedeterminationem decreti divini ad hunc aut illum actum ex voluntate tollere indifferentiam ad operandum, in qua indifferentia posita est libertas: Respondet, Indifferentiam quae opponitur Determinationi ad unum ex necessitate, esse de essentia libertatis & hanc habere liberum arbitrium etiam in eo instanti, quo efficaciter praedeterminatur a Deo ad operandum; imo in ipso instanti quo operatur, non autem esse de essentia libertatis indeterminationem, ut importat potentialitatem, & privationem actus secundi, & ut opponitur determinationi ad alteram partem per modum libertatis, qui in facultate ad utrumlibet consistit.
latin.2076: XVI. Si quis autem urgeat esse de ratione potentiae liberae, ut positis omnibus requisitis ad operandum, possit operari & non operari: sed posito Decreto efficaci Dei praedeterminante nostrum liberum arbitrium ad operandum hoc in particulari, non posse voluntatem non operari illud, quia voluntati Dei nullus potest resistere: Respondet, de ratione potentiae liberae esse ut positis omnibus requisitis ad operandum, possit operari & non operari absolute & simpliciter loquendo: non tamen inconveniens esse, quod ex suppositione voluntatis Divinae efficacis, non possit in sensu composito non operari actum illum, ad quem praedeterminatur a Deo.
latin.2077: XVII. Denique si quis dicat necessitatem opponi libertati: sed si Deus efficaci voluntate nos praedeterminat ad operandum, quamlibet operationem nostram fore necessariam, quoniam necesse est ut si Deus velit aliquid fieri, illud fiat: Respondet, actus omnes praedeterminatos a Deo necessario evenire necessitate Illationis, & ex suppositione ejusdem decreti, non tamen necessitate absoluta, quae libertatem evertit; imo ex eadem praedeterminatione inferri actuale exercitium nostrae libertatis. Quia Deus non solum praedeterminavit, ut voluntas velit tale objectum, sed etiam praedefinivit, ut libere illud velit.
latin.2078: XVIII. Rursus si aliquis instet, necessitatem illam quam inducit decretum divinum tollere libertatem voluntatis creatae, quoniam illud quod est necessarium ex suppositione, efficitur necessarium simpliciter respectu alicujus, quando non est in ejus potestate tollere, vel ponere suppositionem illam, ad quam necessario sequitur actus, qui dicitur ex suppositione necessarius. Sed non est in potestate voluntatis creatae tollere, vel ponere suppositionem illam efficacis decreti voluntatis Dei praedeterminantis liberum arbitrium creatum ad operandum, cum illud decretum sit a solo Deo, & nullo modo dependeat ex libera operatione nostri arbitrii, etiam praecognita per scientiam mediam: ac proinde actus voluntatis qui dicuntur necessarii ex suppositione ejusdem decreti Divini, absolute & simpliciter sunt necessarii, & ita non liberi: Respondet. Quando suppositio antecedens aliquem actum tenet se ex parte primae & universalissimae causae, scilicet Dei, posse aliquid esse necessarium ex suppositione, respectu creatae voluntatis, & tamen liberum illi simpliciter: quamvis non sit in potestate illius ponere, vel tollere suppositionem, ex qua necessario necessitate infallibilitatis istud consequitur. Secus autem contingere, quando suppositio antecedens tenet se ex parte alicujus causae creatae, quae sit voluntati extrinseca. Idque quoniam solus Deus, qui est autor voluntatis creatae, propter suam infinitatem & omnipotentiam, potest illam immutare conformiter ad suam naturam, & movere efficaciter, atque applicare ad producendum actum in particulari, non solum secundum substantiam, sed etiam secundum modum libertatis; quod tamen non potest aliqua causa creata, quia est limitata, & finita, atque inferior ad ipsam voluntatem.
latin.2079: XIX. Verum ista ratio conciliandi libertatem humanam cum providentiae Divinae decretis non satisfacit plurimis Scholae Romanae doctoribus. Itaque inter eos reperiuntur nonnulli qui, ut nodum hunc secent, negant ullos actus liberos, sive naturalis, sive supernaturalis ordinis, ab aeterno a Deo esse praedefinitos; ut nec in tempore ulli tales actus, juxta eorum sensum, a Deo praedeterminantur: quia praedefinitionem pariter ac praedeterminationem voluntatis libertati repugnare existimant. Horum, referente Joanne Strangio, meminit Suares libro tertio de Auxiliis cap. 17. num. 1 & 2.
latin.2080: XX. Similem quoque sententiam quibusdam ex suis tribuit Gabriel Vasquez tomo primo in Thomam disputatione nonagesima nona capite quinto. Ubi referens varia suorum hac de re placita. Demum, inquit, aliqui hac oppressi difficultate dicunt Deum ab aeterno non voluisse opera nostra sigillatim, sed in genere tantum, & in universum definisse paratum esse cum quovis operari, juxta ipsius determinationem. Quibus subjungit illos hanc opinionem amplecti, ut defendant ex praefinitione Dei nullam necessitatem imponi nostrae voluntati contra libertatem suam. Tum etiam quia si necessarium esset Deum praefinire, & velle ab aeterno opera etiam gratiae sigillatim, sequeretur iis qui non operantur, neque vocationi consentiunt, aliquid necessarium deesse ad operandum, scilicet decretum illud, ac proinde mirum non esse si non operarentur, cum sine illo operari non possint.
latin.2081: XXI. Ab his autem non multum absunt quidam alii, qui concedunt quidem Deum singulos hominum actus ab aeterno praefiniisse; sed praefinitionem illam sequi praevisionem futurae determinationis ipsius voluntatis. Nec enim ulla hominum opera, etiam quae sunt bona supernaturaliter, in particulari esse praedefinita absoluto decreto Dei, ante praevisam voluntatis nostrae determinationem, non tantum conditionate, sed etiam absolute futuram. Quae est Doctrina Leonardi Lessii Jesuitae in tractatu de Praedestinatione.
latin.2082: XXII. Et eandem quoque sententiam tribuit Gabriel Vasquez, loco modo citato, Ambrosio Catharino, Antonio de Corduba, Julio Sireno, Osorio, & aliis nonnullis quos docere affirmat, Deum non praefiniisse actus nostros, sive bonos, sive malos secundum substantiam ipsorum, ante praevisam determinationem arbitrii nostri: deinde determinationem ad unam partem potius quam ad aliam, sive in bonis, sive in malis actibus quoad substantiam ipsorum, esse quidem a nobis, & a Deo: sed primam radicem, & causam illius esse liberum arbitrium. Ex quo illos inferre ait, prius intelligi determinationem nostram, quam Dei praedestinationem, & praefinitionem. Et eundem etiam ordinem illos assignare dicit in operibus gratiae, quod attinet ad consensum, & cooperationem: quanquam concedant ante nostram, & Dei cooperationem praecedere gratiam operantem & excitantem, nempe vocationem. Nam, ut refert idem Vasquez, tria instantia distinguunt, Primum in quo voluntas nostra gratia praevenitur; Secundum in quo ipsa se determinet ad consentiendum, vel repugnandum vocationi: Tertium in quo Deus cum illa concurrat. Adeoque ex eorum mente, Deus praescit ad quid voluntas se determinatura sit, tam in operibus gratiae, quam in operibus naturae, antequam cum illa ad hunc, aut illum actum concurrere decernat, & sic antequam ullos actus nostros praefiniat.
latin.2083: XXIII. Facile autem isti conciliant arbitrii nostri libertatem cum decretis divinis; quandoquidem juxta ipsos, decreta Divina sequuntur praevisionem determinationis, quae a voluntate nostra futura est, tanquam prima ejus radice & causa. Ac proinde non magis ex decretis Divinis quam ex Dei praescientia, ulla oritur in nostris actionibus necessitas praecedens, sed solum sequens, quae non tollit, sed integram supponit nostram libertatem.
latin.2084: XXIV. Alii vero hic duplicem distinctionem adhibent. Et primo quidem inter praescientiam futurorum absolutam, & inter praescientiam futurorum conditionatam. Absoluta praescientia est, per quam Deus praevidet hoc, aut illud simpliciter & revera futurum. Praescientia vero conditionata est, per quam Deus praevidet, non quod est simpliciter & absolute futurum; sed quod futurum esset, si haec & illa ponerentur: exempli gratia, quo esset ultro inclinatura & propensura Adami voluntas, si in tali statu crearetur, & offerrentur ipsi haec & illa objecta. Quae est illa scientia quam mediam Scholae vocant, de qua praecedentibus Thesibus abunde egimus.
latin.2085: XXV. Hoc posito concedunt decreta Dei circa actus humanos, vel permittendos, vel efficiendos, in Deo, juxta nostrum concipiendi modum, antecedere praescientiam determinationis voluntatis humanae, quae absolute futura sit. Deus enim verbi causa, ex eorum mente, decrevit permittere ut Adamus pomum vetitum appeteret, & ad actum istum cum eo concurrere, priusquam absolute praeviderit Adami voluntatem eo se determinaturam. Et prius decrevit Paulum gratia sua praevenire, & cum eo ad conversionis actum cooperari, quam absolute praeviderit fore ut Pauli voluntas ad hoc se determinaret.
latin.2086: XXVI. Sed pertendunt Deum de liberis hominum actionibus nihil decrevisse & constituisse, ante quam praevideret in quam partem humana voluntas esset inclinatura, & sese determinatura, posito quod collocaretur in hoc aut illo rerum statu. Nec absolute Deum voluisse ut voluntas eadem has potius eliceret actiones quam illas, priusquam praescierit quid singuli homines acturi essent atque volituri, si tales vel tales agendi occasiones ipsis objicerentur.
latin.2087: XXVII. Haec, scilicet, est eorum doctrina, Deum ante omne decretum de rebus condendis & efficiendis, ab aeterno praevidisse quid posita quacunque conditione futurum & secuturum esset: & infinitas prae oculis habuisse rerum formas, dispositiones ac modos, quibus singulis positis sciebat quid inde foret eventurum. Speciatim vero docent non potuisse Deum ignorare quid eventurum esset, si causas liberas crearet, nempe homines & Angelos, & iis offerri curaret agendi occasiones quae postea oblatae sunt, & postmodum offerentur; & constitueret eos in iis circumstantiis, in quibus postea fuerunt constituti & in posterum constituentur; quid item si ejusmodi circumstantiae infinitis modis variatae fuissent, & longe aliae agendi occasiones oblatae.
latin.2088: XXVIII. Postquam autem Deus sic praevidit & consideravit quid eventurum esset, si homines & angeli collocarentur in his vel illis circumstantiis, & his aut illis objectis ad agendum excitarentur, ac quid inde boni posset elicere, & quomodo haec vel illa ad manifestationem gloriae suae dirigere; tum demum, inquam, Deus, juxta Doctorum istorum sententiam, constituit homines & Angelos creare, in statu in quo postea creati sunt; & procurare ut istae potius quam aliae agendi occasiones iis proponerentur; atque cum iis concurrere ad actiones illas ad quas eorum voluntates, modo concursum suum iis non denegaret, praevidebat sese determinaturas: quod decretum tandem secuta est absoluta praescientia, qua praescivit eos hoc, vel illo modo acturos.
latin.2089: XXIX. Igitur non aliter volunt Deum praeordinavisse & praedefinivisse hominum actiones, quam quia voluit illos in eo statu creare, eaque agendi motiva auxilia, & occasiones iis subministrare, unde consequi praevidebat illos tali modo acturos, hasque potius quam illas volitiones elicituros esse; quanquam semper in eorum potestate maneret, vel sic, vel aliter agere; nulla nempe necessitate per omnia ista ipsis imposita, sic potius quam aliter agendi.
latin.2090: XXX. Hac autem ratione videri posset nil obstare, quominus dicatur Deus praedefinivisse omnes actus liberos, quicunque tandem esse possint. Veruntamen authores istius sententiae distinguunt inter actus bonos & malos. Et quidem actus bonos concedunt recte dici posse aeterno Dei decreto fuisse praedefinitos. Sed de malis aliter sentiunt. Nam quanquam Deus decreverit homines collocare in eo statu in quo praevidebat, per scientiam conditionatam, eos male acturos; eorum tamen actus malos neque vult, neque probat. Dei autem praedefinitio includit, aut praesupponit approbationem Divinae voluntatis. Verum etsi mali actus a Deo non sint praedefiniti, est tamen praedefinita illorum permissio, quia permissio illorum est bona.
latin.2091: XXXI. Haec inter alios est Fonsecae doctrina. Statuit enim. Ante omnem praescientiam actuum liberorum, nullos eorum ab aeterno esse praedefinitos: quia alioqui tolleretur libertas voluntatis creatae: sed post praescientiam futurorum actuum liberorum in statu conditionato, bonos tantum a Deo esse praedefinitos, quia eos solum approbat; etsi autem mali non sint praedefiniti; esse tamen praedefinitam eorum permissionem, quam Deus approbat. In 6. Metaph. cap. 2. quaest. 5. sect. 7.
latin.2092: XXXII. Porro Doctores isti putant non esse difficile providentiae decreta cum arbitrii nostri libertate conciliare, si admittatur ipsorum hypothesis. Nam secundum ipsos Dei Providentia sinit voluntates nostras, secundum propriam cujusque inclinationem agere: nec aliter Deus decrevit hominum animos ducere, & varie inflectere, quam per objectorum intus & extra propositionem; aliasque rationes quae voluntati non tollunt potestatem sic, vel secus agendi; eique permittunt, ut loquuntur Scholae, actionis suae specificationem. Ac proinde tota certitudo decretorum Dei nititur infallibilitate scientiae illius Mediae, per quam Deum praescire asserunt, ante omne voluntatis suae decretum, in quam partem voluntas creata inclinatura & propensura sit, si hae vel istae agendi occasiones ipsi proponantur: non vero aliqua vi atque efficacia, qua voluntas necessario moveatur ut sic agat.
latin.2093: XXXIII. Non tamen haec difficultatis istius solutio satisfacit Gabrieli Vasquez. Probat quidem ille quod dicunt authores sententiae modo expositae, Deum antequam decreta sua condat circa actus liberos, per scientiam quandam conditionatam praescire quo voluntas sit inclinatura, & ad quid se determinatura, si ponantur istae vel illae circumstantiae: sed probare non potest quod concedere non verentur, nempe decreta Dei de actibus liberis in Deo priora esse, secundum nostrum concipiendi modum, absoluta praevisione determinationis ejusdem voluntatis. Nam si concedatur Deum quacunque ratione actus voluntatis nostrae praefinivisse, priusquam absolute praesciat quae futura sit voluntatis inclinatio, & determinatio, putat inde oriri necessitatem quandam antecedentem, quae futurorum actuum libertati repugnat.
latin.2094: XXXIV. Non tamen ad eos accedit, qui putant Deum absolute praescire ad quid voluntas se determinatura sit, priusquam decernat cum illa concurrere ad hunc aut illum actum, & actum ejus ulla ratione praefiniat. Idque quia judicat impossibile esse, voluntatem nostram prius natura operari, aut se determinare, quam Deus cum illa operetur. Unde sequitur, nec in aeternitate intelligi posse illius determinationem, sine decreto Dei concurrendi cum illa. Et praeterea quoniam haec opinio aliquid gratiae Dei cooperanti derogare videtur, Cum enim, inquit, voluntas nostra non tantum indigeat ad operandum excitatione, sed etiam cooperatione gratiae, ut consentiat excitationi: indigebit etiam ut se determinet ad consensum: quomodo ergo in aliquo priori intelligitur determinata sine gratiae cooperatione?
latin.2095: XXXV. Itaque ipse aliud excogitat, nempe Definitionem Dei, quae praefinit opera nostra sigillatim, non praecedere ordine causae determinationem nostrae voluntatis, nec etiam illam sequi; sed eam comitari. Unde colligit necessitatem, quae sequitur positionem decreti Dei, non esse antecedentem, sed comitantem nostram libertatem & determinationem: ac proinde libertatem nostram ea necessitate nec impediri, nec laedi: cum libertati praejudicet sola necessitas praecedens: non vero quae libertatem ipsam, vel sequitur, vel comitatur.
latin.2096: XXXVI. sections.title: Common doctrine: God's eternal will is the cause of all things, and human acts too fall under his immutable decrees
sections.pass_a: THESIS I. The common and received doctrine of Theologians is, and that drawn from manifest documents of Scripture, that the eternal will of God is the cause of all things; and that all things are subject to the immutable Decrees of divine providence, even human acts; and that nothing is done, not only by brute or inanimate causes, but also by men and Angels, except according to the eternal preordination and determination of God.
pass_b: It is the common, accepted teaching of theologians, drawn from the plain witness of Scripture, that God's eternal will is the cause of all things. Everything, human acts included, is subject to the unchangeable decrees of God's providence.
Nothing happens, whether by brute and lifeless causes or by men and angels, except in accordance with God's eternal preordination and determination.

sections.title: The difficulty: no one resists God's will, so freedom and the will's indetermination seem lost
sections.pass_a: II. But from this freedom seems to perish altogether, as much in Angels as in men. For no one can resist the divine will. And so if God wills that Angels and men do what they do, they cannot do otherwise, and so they do not act freely, nor are they lords of their own acts. Then if the actions of the human will are determined by immutable decrees of God, all indetermination of the will seems to be taken away, and the indifference in acting, in which the nature of freedom consists.
pass_b: Yet this seems to destroy freedom entirely, in angels and in men alike. No one can resist God's will. If God wills that angels and men do what they do, they cannot act otherwise; so they do not act freely and are not masters of their own acts.

Again, if the actions of the human will are determined by God's unchangeable decrees, the will seems to lose all indetermination, and with it the indifference in acting in which the essence of freedom consists.

sections.title: Some scholastics confessed it beyond reason in this life, notably Cardinal Cajetan
sections.pass_a: III. Of which number was Cardinal Cajetan, a man very celebrated among the Scholastics. For he, however acute and subtle, could never satisfy himself in this matter, and thought the concord of free choice with divine providence to be inexplicable and not intelligible in this life, as may be seen in his commentaries on the first part of Thomas, quest. 22, art. 4.
pass_b: Some scholastics found this difficulty so hard that they frankly confessed their ignorance on this point. They judged it beyond the reach of the human mind so long as the mind is burdened with this mortal body.

One of them was Cardinal Cajetan, a very famous figure among the scholastics. Sharp and subtle as he was, he could never satisfy himself here. He held that the harmony of free choice with God's providence cannot be explained or understood in this life, as his commentary on the first part of Thomas, question 22, article 4, shows.

sections.pass_a: IV. Yet other Theologians of the Roman School are confident that they can untie this knot, and to this end they search out and devise various things. For not all think the same, either concerning the Divine Decrees, or concerning the nature of human freedom.

sections.title: The later Thomists: every free act predetermined by absolute decree before any foreseen determination (Alvarez)
sections.pass_a: V. And first those who are called the more recent Thomists teach that whatever things happen and are done in the world, and therefore also the free acts of the will, have been singly predetermined and predefined by God, and that by an absolute and efficacious will, prior in reason to God's foreseeing any determination of the created will, whether future absolutely or under condition. This is the express opinion, among others, of Diego Alvarez, Archbishop of Trani and Salpi, in the summary of the Work on the helps of divine grace, book two, chapter five, which begins with these words, From the divine letters, if they are attentively weighed, we have that God by his absolute and efficacious will predetermined all acts, even free ones, in particular, future in time, prior in the sign of reason, to the divine intellect's knowing those acts to be future, even on the hypothesis that the created will were set in such an order of things, and in such circumstances.
pass_b: To begin with the so-called recent Thomists: on their teaching, everything that occurs and is carried out in the world, and so also every free act of the will, was individually predetermined and predefined by God. God did this by an absolute and efficacious will, prior in reason to his foreseeing any determination of the created will, whether it was to come about absolutely or only on some condition.

This is the express view of Diego Alvarez, Archbishop of Trani and Salpi, among others, in the summary of his work on the helps of divine grace, book 2, chapter 5, which begins: 'From the sacred writings, if they are carefully weighed, we have it that God by his absolute and efficacious will predetermined all acts in particular, free ones included, that are to come about in time.

He did so prior in the sign of reason to the divine intellect's knowing that those acts would come about, even on the hypothesis that the created will were placed in such an order of things and in such circumstances.'

sections.title: So Matthaeus de Rispolis, and Estius agrees
sections.pass_a: VI. The same doctrine is delivered by Matthaeus de Rispolis in the treatise whose title is, The State of the controversy of predefinitions and predeterminations with free choice. For there in book one, question one, he teaches at length and strives to prove that there are in God eternal predefinitions and predeterminations of the acts of the will, and that in particular, and by an absolute decree, which presupposes no conditional knowledge of the future determination of the will itself, if it be placed in such a state of things. And with these William Estius also agrees, as is manifestly gathered from those things which are read in him on the thirty-ninth distinction of the first book of the sentences, and on the twenty-fourth of the second book.
pass_b: Matthaeus de Rispolis teaches the same doctrine in his treatise entitled The State of the Controversy over Predefinitions and Predeterminations in Relation to Free Choice. In book 1, question 1, he argues at length that there are in God eternal predefinitions and predeterminations of the will's acts, in particular and by an absolute decree.

That decree, he holds, presupposes no conditional knowledge of how the will would determine itself if placed in such a state of things. William Estius agrees with them too, as is clear from what he writes on distinction 39 of the first book of the Sentences and on distinction 24 of the second book.

sections.title: Evil acts too are predefined as to their positive reality; their malice only permitted (Alvarez)
sections.pass_a: VII. Nor do those authors except from this eternal predetermination of God the evil acts of the will themselves, which also they will to have been predefined by an absolute and efficacious decree, at least as to that which in those acts is real and positive; for the malice itself, which is nothing other than the privation of due rectitude, they confess not to have been efficaciously decreed by God, but only permitted. This is especially to be seen in Diego Alvarez in the summary on helps now cited, book two, chapter nine, whose beginning is this, The things which have been said concerning the predetermination of the will to good acts, ought to be extended to the act of sin insofar as it is act and being. Whence whatever of entity is found in any act of sin whatsoever, even though otherwise it be intrinsically evil, ought to be reduced to God as to the first cause premoving and predetermining the created will to such an act, insofar as it is act, and according as it is being.
pass_b: These authors do not exempt even the will's evil acts from this eternal predetermination of God. They hold that these too were predefined by an absolute and efficacious decree, at least as to what is real and positive in them. The malice itself, which is nothing but the privation of due rightness, they admit God did not efficaciously decree but only permitted.

This is seen especially in Diego Alvarez, in the summary on the helps of grace already cited, book 2, chapter 9, which begins: 'What has been said about the predetermination of the will to good acts must be extended to the act of sin insofar as it is an act and a being.

Hence whatever entity is found in any act of sin, even if that act is otherwise intrinsically evil, must be traced back to God as the first cause, who premoves and predetermines the created will to such an act insofar as it is an act and insofar as it is a being.'

sections.title: Yet they hold this leaves contingency intact: God decreed not only the event but its free mode
sections.pass_a: VIII. But although God, according to their mind, has by his eternal decree predetermined and predefined whatever things are done in time by any causes, they contend that this does not at all hinder many things from being done not necessarily, but contingently and freely: since the eternal providence of God has not prepared necessary causes for all events and effects, but for some free or contingent causes; and has not only determined that this or that be done, but also the mode in which each thing should be done, and so willed that some things be done necessarily, but others contingently and freely. And thus so far is it from being the case that the eternal Providence of God takes away the freedom of human acts, that on the contrary whatever there is of freedom and contingency in things is to be referred to him as to the first cause: because, namely, God not only willed things to be, but also by his will established and defined the mode and manner in which each ought to be.
pass_b: On their view, God by his eternal decree predetermined and predefined whatever is done in time by any cause. Even so, they maintain that nothing prevents many things from happening not by necessity but contingently and freely.

God's eternal providence did not provide necessary causes for every event and effect; for some it provided free or contingent causes. Nor did it determine only that this or that should happen; it also determined the way each thing should happen. So God willed some things to happen necessarily, and others contingently and freely.

Far from removing the freedom of human acts, then, God's eternal providence is the first cause to which whatever freedom and contingency there is in things must be traced. For God willed not only that things should be, but also by his will settled and defined the mode and manner in which each should be.

sections.title: God decreed not only that men act but that they act freely, choosing by their own judgement with power for the opposite
sections.pass_a: IX. And so that God decreed from eternity that men should do this or that, and by their will be borne toward these or those objects, according to the sense of those Doctors nothing hinders the freedom of men: because God did not simply decree that they should do this or that, but also that they should do it freely, that is, that from the judgement of their own reason they should choose this or that as most fitting and advantageous to themselves, and indeed in such a way that from a different judgement they could choose the opposite; in which, according to their opinion, human freedom properly consists, which therefore the determination of the divine decree does not overthrow.
pass_b: So, in these doctors' view, God's having decreed from eternity that men should do this or that, and that their wills should be drawn to these or those objects, is no obstacle to human freedom. God did not decree simply that they should do this or that, but that they should do it freely.

That is, they were to choose this or that by the judgement of their own reason as most fitting and advantageous for themselves, and in such a way that, judging differently, they could choose the opposite. On their view human freedom properly consists in this, so the determination made by the divine decree does not overturn it.

For they judge, as they speak, that it is impertinent to free choice whether it has its election impressed on it by a prior cause, or not: provided that election be made from the judgement of the practical intellect, which can consider diverse reasons of good about opposites, and propose them to the will.
pass_b: In their phrase, it is 'irrelevant' to free choice whether its choosing is impressed on it by a prior cause or not.
What matters is that the choice comes from a judgement of the practical intellect, which is able to weigh different kinds of good on opposite sides and set them before the will.

sections.title: Independence from a prior cause belongs to God alone; free creatures depend on the first cause as necessary ones do
sections.pass_a: XI. But if anyone says that the name of free choice designates a cause independent of some prior one, in respect of its free action, they answer that this is falsely and undeservedly assumed as true, and that free choice of that kind belongs to God alone, who is altogether independent of a superior cause. But that free creatures depend no less on the first Cause in their free acts, than necessary causes in necessary acts.
pass_b: Someone may say that 'free choice' means a cause that, in its free action, is independent of any prior cause. They reply that this is assumed as true falsely and without warrant.

Free choice of that kind belongs to God alone, who is wholly independent of any higher cause. Free creatures depend on the first cause in their free acts no less than necessary causes do in their necessary acts.

sections.title: The decree determines the act but leaves the faculty flexible: true in the divided, not the composite sense
sections.pass_a: XII. But to that which is objected, that, a divine decree concerning some act of the human will being posited, the human will cannot act otherwise, and so its indifference in acting, in which freedom is placed, is taken away, they answer, that indeed these do not stand together, that God has decreed the will to do something, but the will does not do it, or does otherwise: but yet the decree of God does not hinder that there remains in the will a power of acting otherwise: since the decree of God indeed determines the act, but leaves the faculty flexible to the opposite. And therefore when a man does something according to the decree of God, it can truly be said that he can not do it, and do otherwise, because, namely, God decreed indeed that he do this, but yet that he so do it that he remains able to act otherwise: And so, although in the composite sense it is not true, the divine decree being posited, that the will can act, or not act, yet it is true in the divided sense: because with the divine decree the opposite act indeed does not stand, but yet the faculty for the opposite act stands perfectly well.
pass_b: It is objected that once God has decreed some act of the human will, the will cannot act otherwise, so its indifference in acting, where freedom lies, is removed. They answer that it cannot both be true that God decreed the will should do something and that the will does not do it or does something else.

Yet God's decree does not prevent the will from keeping the power to act otherwise. The decree determines the act, but leaves the faculty able to turn to the opposite. So when a man does something in keeping with God's decree, it can truly be said that he is able not to do it and to act otherwise. God decreed that he should do this, but should do it in such a way that he remains able to act otherwise.

Thus, granted the divine decree, it is not true in the composite sense that the will can act or not act; but it is true in the divided sense. The opposite act cannot stand together with the divine decree, but the faculty for the opposite act stands with it perfectly well.

sections.title: If pressed that God's decrees would be frustrated, they deny it: had man acted otherwise, God would have decreed otherwise
sections.pass_a: XIII. But if someone urges that, a divine decree concerning some action being posited, it can in no way be said that a man can act otherwise, since from that it would follow that the decrees of God could be frustrated and be void, which is simply impossible, they deny that consequence, because if man acted otherwise, which is supposed possible, God would have decreed otherwise. Nor do they think it conflicts with the immutability of the divine decrees that man, while he executes them, keeps the power of acting otherwise, but only if someone should say that it can happen that a man does the contrary of that which has been decreed by God, which those Theologians by no means say.
pass_b: Someone may press the point: granted God's decree about some action, it cannot be said at all that a man can act otherwise, since it would follow that God's decrees could be thwarted and made void, which is utterly impossible. They deny the inference. If the man acted otherwise, which is assumed to be possible, God would have decreed otherwise.

They do not think it conflicts with the unchangeableness of God's decrees that a man, while carrying them out, keeps the power to act otherwise. It would conflict only if someone said that a man can end up doing the contrary of what God has decreed, and these theologians say no such thing.

sections.title: Estius and Alvarez: being able to will differs from actually willing; the decree is needed only for the act
sections.pass_a: XIV. Many things similar to these may be read in William Estius in the places cited before, and in Diego Alvarez in the summary on Helps book two chapter six, where he dissolves the objections against the predetermination of the will proceeding from the extrinsic decree of God. For to that which he objects to himself, that from his opinion it follows that man cannot will, except that which God by efficacious decree wills him to will: nor can he work except acts predetermined by God; and so we do not freely will what we will, but from absolute necessity, because we cannot do otherwise, if God wills that we do it, And by the same reason those acts which are under precept are not freely omitted by us: Because if it is necessary for this, that we do such an act, that God has predetermined our will to the same act, we cannot do it, if God by his absolute and efficacious decree has not predetermined that act to be done by us. He answers, that as it is one thing to be able to run, another to run in act; so it is one thing to be able to will, or to produce some act in particular; another to produce it in fact: therefore that a man may truly be able to will some object, it is not required that there has preceded from eternity in God an absolute and efficacious decree predetermining his free choice to will the same object; although that is required that he will it in act. Whence from this that there was not such a decree in God, it does not follow that man cannot will such an object absolutely speaking: but it only follows that in fact he does not will it. Nor also does it follow that, if God has predetermined me to will this in particular, it is not, absolutely speaking, in my power to will another thing; although from the supposition of the efficacious divine will, it is impossible in the composite sense that I will another object.
pass_b: Much of the same kind can be read in William Estius in the places cited above, and in Diego Alvarez, summary on the helps of grace, book 2, chapter 6. There Alvarez answers the objections against a predetermination of the will that comes from God's external decree.

He raises this objection against himself. On his view, man can will only what God by an efficacious decree wills him to will, and can perform only acts God has predetermined. So we do not will freely what we will, but by absolute necessity, since we cannot do otherwise if God wills that we do it.

By the same reasoning, the acts commanded of us are not freely left undone. For if God's having predetermined our will to an act is required for us to do it, we cannot do it unless God by his absolute and efficacious decree has predetermined that we shall do it.

He answers that being able to run is one thing and actually running another. In the same way, being able to will or to produce some particular act is one thing, and actually producing it is another. For a man truly to be able to will an object, it is not required that an absolute and efficacious decree should have preceded in God from eternity, predetermining his free choice to will that object. That is required only for him actually to will it.

So from the absence of such a decree in God it does not follow that, absolutely speaking, the man cannot will the object; it follows only that he does not in fact will it. Nor does it follow that, if God has predetermined me to will this particular thing, it is not in my power, absolutely speaking, to will something else. Granted God's efficacious will, however, it is impossible in the composite sense that I should will another object.

sections.title: Indifference opposed to necessity is of freedom's essence; indetermination implying potentiality is not
sections.pass_a: XV. But to that which is objected, that the predetermination of the divine decree to this or that act takes away from the will indifference to working, in which indifference freedom is placed: He answers, that Indifference which is opposed to Determination to one from necessity, is of the essence of freedom, and that free choice has this even in that instant in which it is efficaciously predetermined by God to work; nay, in the very instant in which it works; but that indetermination is not of the essence of freedom, as it imports potentiality, and privation of second act, and as it is opposed to determination to one part by way of freedom, which consists in a faculty for either.
pass_b: It is objected that the predetermination of the divine decree to this or that act takes from the will its indifference to acting, in which freedom lies. Alvarez answers that the indifference opposed to being determined to one thing by necessity does belong to the essence of freedom.

Free choice has this indifference even at the moment when God efficaciously predetermines it to act, indeed at the very moment it acts. What does not belong to the essence of freedom is indetermination in the sense that implies potentiality and the lack of a second act, and that is opposed to being determined to one side in the manner proper to freedom, which consists in a capacity for either side.

sections.pass_a: XVI. But if anyone urges that it is of the nature of a free power that, all things requisite for working being posited, it can work and not work: but, an efficacious Decree of God being posited predetermining our free choice to work this in particular, the will cannot not work it, because no one can resist the will of God: He answers, that it is of the nature of a free power that, all things requisite for working being posited, it can work and not work absolutely and simply speaking: but yet it is not unfitting, that from the supposition of the efficacious Divine will, it cannot in the composite sense not work that act, to which it is predetermined by God.
pass_b: Someone may insist that a free power, by its nature, is able to act and not act once everything required for acting is in place. Yet once God's efficacious decree predetermines our free choice to do this particular thing, the will cannot fail to do it, for no one can resist God's will.

Alvarez answers that a free power, by its nature, is able to act and not act, with everything required for acting in place, speaking absolutely and without qualification. It is no absurdity, however, that granted God's efficacious will, it cannot in the composite sense fail to perform the act to which God predetermines it.

sections.pass_a: XVII. Finally if anyone says that necessity is opposed to freedom: but if God by an efficacious will predetermines us to working, any operation of ours whatever will be necessary, since it is necessary that if God wills something to be done, it is done: He answers, that all acts predetermined by God come about necessarily by necessity of Inference, and from the supposition of the same decree, yet not by absolute necessity, which overthrows freedom; nay, from the same predetermination is inferred the actual exercise of our freedom. Because God not only predetermined that the will will such an object, but also predefined that it will it freely.
pass_b: Lastly, someone may say that necessity is opposed to freedom; and if God by an efficacious will predetermines us to act, every one of our actions will be necessary, since whatever God wills to happen must happen. Alvarez answers that all acts God has predetermined do come about necessarily, but by necessity of inference, given the supposition of that decree.

They do not come about by absolute necessity, which overturns freedom. In fact, the same predetermination implies the actual exercise of our freedom. For God predetermined not only that the will should will such an object, but also predefined that it should will it freely.

sections.title: Objection: a supposition outside the will's power makes the act simply necessary; answer: not when the supposition is on God's side
sections.pass_a: XVIII. Again if anyone insists that that necessity which the divine decree induces takes away the freedom of the created will, since that which is necessary from supposition is made necessary simply in respect of someone, when it is not in his power to take away, or posit that supposition, to which the act necessarily follows, which is called necessary from supposition. But it is not in the power of the created will to take away, or posit that supposition of the efficacious decree of the will of God predetermining created free choice to working, since that decree is from God alone, and in no way depends on the free operation of our choice, even foreknown by middle knowledge: and therefore the acts of the will which are said to be necessary from supposition of the same Divine decree, are absolutely and simply necessary, and so not free: He answers. When the supposition antecedent to some act holds itself on the part of the first and most universal cause, namely God, something can be necessary from supposition, in respect of the created will, and yet free to it simply: although it is not in its power to posit, or take away the supposition, from which by necessity of infallibility it necessarily follows. But that it happens otherwise, when the antecedent supposition holds itself on the part of some created cause, which is extrinsic to the will. And this because God alone, who is the author of the created will, on account of his infinity and omnipotence, can change it conformably to its nature, and move it efficaciously, and apply it to producing an act in particular, not only according to the substance, but also according to the mode of freedom; which yet a created cause cannot, because it is limited, and finite, and inferior to the will itself.
pass_b: Someone may press further that the necessity introduced by the divine decree removes the freedom of the created will. What is necessary on a supposition becomes simply necessary for a given agent when it is not in his power to remove or establish the supposition from which the act, called necessary on that supposition, follows necessarily.

But it is not in the created will's power to remove or establish the supposition of God's efficacious decree predetermining created free choice to act. That decree comes from God alone and in no way depends on the free working of our choice, not even as foreknown by middle knowledge. So the will's acts that are called necessary on the supposition of that decree are necessary absolutely and simply, and therefore not free.

Alvarez answers that when the supposition preceding an act lies on the side of the first and most universal cause, namely God, something can be necessary on a supposition with respect to the created will and yet free for it without qualification. This holds even though it is not in the will's power to establish or remove the supposition from which the act necessarily follows by the necessity of infallibility.

It is otherwise, he says, when the preceding supposition lies on the side of some created cause external to the will. Only God, the author of the created will, can by his infinity and omnipotence change it in keeping with its nature, move it efficaciously, and apply it to produce a particular act, not only as to its substance but also as to its free mode. A created cause cannot do this, because it is limited, finite and lower than the will itself.

sections.title: Vasquez reports some who say God foreordained our works only in general, lest necessity or a lack of the decree follow
sections.pass_a: XX. A similar opinion also Gabriel Vasquez attributes to some of his own, in the first tome on Thomas, disputation ninety-nine, chapter five. Where reporting various tenets of his own on this matter. Finally, he says, some, oppressed by this difficulty, say that God from eternity did not will our works singly, but only in general, and defined in universal that he is ready to work with anyone, according to his determination. To which he subjoins that they embrace this opinion, that they may defend that from the foreordination of God no necessity is imposed on our will against its freedom. Then also because if it were necessary that God foreordain, and will from eternity even the works of grace singly, it would follow that to those who do not work, nor consent to the calling, something necessary for working is lacking, namely that decree, and therefore that it is no wonder if they did not work, since without it they could not work.
pass_b: Gabriel Vasquez attributes a similar view to some of his own school, in volume 1 on Thomas, disputation 99, chapter 5, where he reports their various positions on this question. 'Finally,' he says, 'some, overwhelmed by this difficulty, say that God from eternity did not will our works one by one, but only in general, and determined in a universal way that he is ready to act with anyone according to that person's determination.'

Vasquez adds that they adopt this view in order to maintain that God's foreordination imposes no necessity on our will against its freedom. A further reason is this. If God had to foreordain and will from eternity even the works of grace one by one, those who do not act and do not consent to the call would lack something necessary for acting, namely that decree. It would then be no wonder that they did not act, since without it they could not.

sections.title: Vasquez assigns the same to Catharinus, Cordoba, Sirenus, Osorio: free choice the first root; three instants in works of grace
sections.pass_a: XXII. And the same opinion also Gabriel Vasquez, in the place just cited, attributes to Ambrose Catharinus, Antonio de Cordoba, Julius Sirenus, Osorio, and some others whom he affirms to teach, that God did not foreordain our acts, whether good, or evil, according to their substance, before the foreseen determination of our choice: then that the determination to one part rather than to another, whether in good, or in evil acts as to their substance, is indeed from us, and from God: but that the first root, and cause of it is free choice. From which he says they infer, that our determination is understood before the predestination, and foreordination of God. And he says that they assign the same order also in the works of grace, as far as pertains to consent, and cooperation: although they concede that before our, and God's cooperation there precedes operating and exciting grace, namely calling. For, as the same Vasquez reports, they distinguish three instants, The First in which our will is prevented by grace; The Second in which it determines itself to consenting, or resisting the calling: The Third in which God concurs with it. And so according to their mind, God foreknows to what the will will determine itself, as well in the works of grace, as in the works of nature, before he decrees to concur with it to this, or that act, and so before he foreordains any acts of ours.
pass_b: In the same place Vasquez attributes the same view to Ambrose Catharinus, Antonio de Cordoba, Julius Sirenus, Osorio and some others. They teach, he says, that God did not foreordain our acts, good or evil, as to their substance, before he foresaw how our choice would determine itself. The determination to one side rather than the other, in good or evil acts as to their substance, comes indeed both from us and from God, but its first root and cause is free choice.

From this, Vasquez says, they infer that our determination is understood to come before God's predestination and foreordination. They assign the same order, he says, in the works of grace as regards consent and cooperation, though they grant that operating and arousing grace, that is, the call, comes before both our cooperation and God's.

As Vasquez reports, they distinguish three instants. In the first our will is anticipated by grace. In the second it determines itself to consent to the call or to resist it. In the third God concurs with it. So on their view God foreknows what the will is going to determine itself to, in works of grace as in works of nature, before he decrees to concur with it in this or that act, and so before he foreordains any of our acts.

sections.pass_a: XXIII. But these easily reconcile the freedom of our choice with the divine decrees; since according to them, the Divine decrees follow the prevision of the determination which is to be from our will, as its first root and cause. And therefore no more from the Divine decrees than from God's foreknowledge does any preceding necessity arise in our actions, but only a following one, which does not take away, but supposes entire our freedom.
pass_b: These men find it easy to reconcile the freedom of our choice with God's decrees. On their view the divine decrees follow God's foresight of the determination that will come from our will as its first root and cause.

So the divine decrees, no more than God's foreknowledge, give rise to any preceding necessity in our actions. They produce only a consequent necessity, which does not remove our freedom but presupposes it intact.

sections.title: Others distinguish absolute and conditional foreknowledge; the latter is the middle knowledge treated above
sections.pass_a: XXIV. But others here apply a double distinction. And first between absolute foreknowledge of futures, and conditional foreknowledge of futures. Absolute foreknowledge is that by which God foresees this, or that simply and really future. But conditional foreknowledge is that by which God foresees, not what is simply and absolutely future; but what would be future, if these and those things were posited: for example, whither the will of Adam would of its own accord incline and be inclined, if it were created in such a state, and these and those objects were offered to it. Which is that knowledge which the Schools call middle, concerning which we have treated abundantly in the preceding Theses.
pass_b: Others, however, use a twofold distinction here. The first is between absolute and conditional foreknowledge of future things. Absolute foreknowledge is that by which God foresees this or that as simply and really future.

Conditional foreknowledge is that by which God foresees not what is simply and absolutely future, but what would be future if this or that were in place. An example is the direction in which Adam's will would of its own accord lean and tend if it were created in such a state and these or those objects were put before it. This is the knowledge the schools call middle knowledge, which we dealt with at length in the preceding theses.

sections.pass_a: XXV. This being posited, they concede that the decrees of God concerning human acts, either to be permitted, or to be effected, precede in God, according to our mode of conceiving, the foreknowledge of the determination of the human will, which is to be absolutely future. For God for example, according to their mind, decreed to permit that Adam should desire the forbidden apple, and to concur with him to that act, before he absolutely foresaw that Adam's will would determine itself to it. And he decreed to prevent Paul with his grace, and to cooperate with him to the act of conversion, before he absolutely foresaw that Paul's will would determine itself to this.
pass_b: On this basis they grant that God's decrees about human acts, whether to permit them or to bring them about, come before his foreknowledge of the human will's absolutely future determination, according to our way of conceiving things in God.

On their view, for example, God decreed to permit Adam to desire the forbidden fruit, and to concur with him in that act, before he absolutely foresaw that Adam's will would determine itself to it. Likewise he decreed to anticipate Paul with his grace and to cooperate with him in the act of conversion before he absolutely foresaw that Paul's will would determine itself to it.

sections.title: Their doctrine: before any decree God foresaw what would follow under every condition, and above all with free creatures
sections.pass_a: XXVII. This, namely, is their doctrine, that God before every decree concerning things to be founded and effected, foresaw from eternity what, any condition whatever being posited, would be future and would follow: and had before his eyes infinite forms, dispositions and modes of things, each of which being posited he knew what would thence come to pass. But specially they teach that God could not be ignorant what would come to pass, if he created free causes, namely men and Angels, and took care that occasions of acting were offered to them which afterwards were offered, and hereafter will be offered; and set them in those circumstances, in which afterwards they were set and in time to come will be set; what likewise if circumstances of that kind had been varied in infinite ways, and far other occasions of acting offered.
pass_b: Their teaching, then, is this. Before any decree about creating and bringing about things, God foresaw from eternity what would come about and follow given any condition at all. He had before his eyes countless forms, arrangements and modes of things, and for each of them he knew what would result if it were put in place.

In particular they teach that God could not be ignorant of what would happen if he created free causes, namely men and angels, and saw to it that they were offered the occasions for acting that were later offered and will be offered hereafter, and placed them in the circumstances in which they were later placed and will be placed in future. Nor could he be ignorant of what would happen if such circumstances had been varied in countless ways and quite different occasions for acting had been offered.

sections.title: Only after this foresight did God decree to create, to arrange the occasions, and to concur; absolute foreknowledge follows the decree
sections.pass_a: XXVIII. But after God thus foresaw and considered what would come to pass, if men and angels were placed in these or those circumstances, and were excited to act by these or those objects, and what good he could draw out from it, and how he could direct these or those things to the manifestation of his glory; then at last, I say, God, according to the opinion of these Doctors, determined to create men and Angels, in the state in which they were afterwards created; and to procure that these rather than other occasions of acting should be proposed to them; and to concur with them to those actions to which he foresaw their wills, provided he did not deny them his concurrence, would determine themselves: which decree at length absolute foreknowledge followed, by which he foreknew that they would act in this, or that way.
pass_b: God thus foresaw and considered what would happen if men and angels were placed in these or those circumstances and prompted to act by these or those objects, what good he could bring out of it, and how he could direct these things or those to the display of his glory. Only then, I say, on these doctors' view, did God resolve to create men and angels in the state in which they were afterwards created.

He resolved also to arrange that these occasions for acting rather than others should be put before them, and to concur with them in the actions to which he foresaw their wills would determine themselves, provided he did not withhold his concurrence. Finally, this decree was followed by the absolute foreknowledge by which he foreknew that they would act in this way or that.

Yet the authors of this opinion distinguish between good and evil acts. And indeed good acts they concede can rightly be said to have been predefined by the eternal decree of God. But of evil ones they think otherwise. For although God decreed to place men in that state in which he foresaw, by conditional knowledge, that they would act evilly; yet their evil acts he neither wills, nor approves. But the predefinition of God includes, or presupposes the approval of the Divine will. But although evil acts are not predefined by God, yet their permission is predefined, because their permission is good.
pass_b: On this account it might seem that nothing prevents us from saying that God predefined all free acts, whatever they may turn out to be. The authors of this view, however, distinguish between good and evil acts. Good acts, they grant, can rightly be said to have been predefined by God's eternal decree. About evil acts they think otherwise.

God did decree to place men in the state in which he foresaw, by conditional knowledge, that they would act badly. Yet he neither wills nor approves their evil acts, and God's predefinition includes or presupposes the approval of the divine will. So although evil acts are not predefined by God, their permission is predefined, because permitting them is good.

sections.title: They hold the decrees easy to reconcile with freedom: providence moves the will only by proposing objects and reasons; certainty rests on middle knowledge
sections.pass_a: XXXII. Further those Doctors think it is not difficult to reconcile the decrees of providence with the freedom of our choice, if their hypothesis is admitted. For according to them the Providence of God allows our wills to act according to the proper inclination of each: nor has God decreed to lead and variously bend the minds of men otherwise than through the proposal of objects within and without; and other reasons which do not take from the will the power of acting thus, or otherwise; and permit it, as the Schools speak, the specification of its action. And therefore the whole certainty of the decrees of God rests on the infallibility of that Middle knowledge, through which they assert that God foreknows, before every decree of his will, to which part the created will would incline and be inclined, if these or those occasions of acting were proposed to it: not truly on some force and efficacy, by which the will is necessarily moved so to act.
pass_b: These doctors also think that, once their hypothesis is admitted, it is not hard to reconcile the decrees of providence with the freedom of our choice. On their view God's providence lets our wills act according to each one's own inclination.

God has not decreed to lead men's minds and turn them in various directions by any means other than setting objects before them, within and without, and other inducements that do not take from the will its power to act this way or otherwise. These leave to the will, as the schools put it, the specification of its action.

So the whole certainty of God's decrees rests on the infallibility of that middle knowledge, by which, they claim, God foreknows before any decree of his will which way the created will would lean and tend if these or those occasions for acting were put before it. It does not rest on any force or efficacy by which the will is necessarily moved to act so.

sections.pass_a: XXXIII. Yet this solution of that difficulty does not satisfy Gabriel Vasquez. He indeed approves what the authors of the opinion just set out say, that God before he frames his decrees about free acts, foreknows by a certain conditional knowledge whither the will would incline, and to what it would determine itself, if these or those circumstances were posited: but he cannot approve what they do not fear to concede, namely that the decrees of God concerning free acts are prior in God, according to our mode of conceiving, to the absolute prevision of the determination of the same will. For if it be conceded that God by any manner whatever foreordained the acts of our will, before he absolutely foreknows what will be the inclination, and determination of the will, he thinks that from that there arises a certain antecedent necessity, which is repugnant to the freedom of future acts.
pass_b: Gabriel Vasquez, however, is not satisfied with this solution of the difficulty. He accepts what the authors of the view just set out say: that before God frames his decrees about free acts, he foreknows by a kind of conditional knowledge which way the will would lean and what it would determine itself to, if these or those circumstances were in place.

What he cannot accept is what they do not hesitate to grant, namely that God's decrees about free acts come in God, according to our way of conceiving, before his absolute foresight of that same will's determination. If it is granted that God in any way foreordained the acts of our will before he absolutely foreknows what its inclination and determination will be, Vasquez thinks there arises from this a kind of antecedent necessity that is incompatible with the freedom of future acts.

sections.title: Nor does Vasquez side with those who put absolute foreknowledge of the will's determination before God's decree to concur
sections.pass_a: XXXIV. Yet he does not go over to those who think that God absolutely foreknows to what the will will determine itself, before he decrees to concur with it to this or that act, and by any manner foreordains its act. And this because he judges it impossible, that our will should work, or determine itself prior in nature, before God works with it. Whence it follows, that not even in eternity can its determination be understood, without the decree of God to concur with it. And moreover because this opinion seems to derogate something from the cooperating grace of God, For since, he says, our will needs for working not only excitation, but also the cooperation of grace, that it may consent to the excitation: it will need it also that it may determine itself to consent: how then is it understood as determined in some prior without the cooperation of grace?
pass_b: Yet he does not join those who think God absolutely foreknows what the will is going to determine itself to before he decrees to concur with it in this or that act, and before he in any way foreordains its act. His reason is that he judges it impossible for our will to act or determine itself prior in nature to God's acting with it. It follows that not even in eternity can the will's determination be understood apart from God's decree to concur with it.

A further reason is that this view seems to take something away from God's cooperating grace. 'Our will,' he says, 'needs for acting not only to be aroused but also the cooperation of grace in order to consent to that arousing. So it will need that cooperation in order to determine itself to consent as well. How then can it be understood as determined at some prior moment without the cooperation of grace?'

sections.title: Vasquez's own view: God's definition of our acts neither precedes nor follows the will's determination but accompanies it
sections.pass_a: XXXV. Therefore he himself devises something else, namely that the Definition of God, which foreordains our works singly, does not precede in order of cause the determination of our will, nor yet follow it; but accompanies it. Whence he gathers that the necessity which follows the positing of the decree of God is not antecedent, but accompanying our freedom and determination: and therefore that our freedom by that necessity is neither impeded, nor hurt: since only preceding necessity prejudices freedom: not truly that which either follows, or accompanies freedom itself.
pass_b: So Vasquez devises something else of his own. God's definition, which foreordains our works one by one, neither comes before the determination of our will in the order of causes nor follows it, but accompanies it.

From this he concludes that the necessity which follows once God's decree is posited is not antecedent to our freedom and determination but accompanies them. So our freedom is neither hindered nor harmed by that necessity, since only a preceding necessity damages freedom, not one that follows or accompanies it.

sections.title: His ground: God's cooperation is simultaneous with our consent, so decree and foresight of our determination are conceived together
sections.pass_a: XXXVI. But the foundation of his opinion is, that on the part of God no operation, which precedes the consent of our will, imposes necessity on the will that it consent: but that cooperation of God, through which he effects the very consent of our will, in no way precedes the determination of our will, but is together with it in time, nature, and reason. Whence it follows that the decree of God concerning working that consent cannot be prior to the prevision of the determination of the human will: because things which are altogether together in time cannot have the order of prior and posterior in the foreknowledge and decrees of God. From which things he concludes that no free work of our will was predefined by God, before the foreseen free determination of our will: but that the prevision of that determination, and the decree of God predefining the act of our will, ought to be conceived together in God.
pass_b: The basis of his view is this. On God's side, no working that precedes our will's consent imposes on the will a necessity to consent. The cooperation of God by which he brings about our will's very consent in no way precedes our will's determination; it exists together with it in time, in nature and in reason.

It follows that God's decree to bring about that consent cannot come before his foresight of the human will's determination. Things that exist wholly together in time cannot have an order of prior and posterior in God's foreknowledge and decrees.

From this he concludes that no free work of our will was predefined by God before he foresaw our will's free determination. Rather, the foresight of that determination and God's decree predefining our will's act must be conceived as together in God.
